concept: Carry equals leverage times yield minus borrow cost

claims.text: Y differs in durability by source, and that sets how much of L×Y a planner can rely on. Kamino separates structural yield (staking 'exists whether or not anyone is using Multiply') from fee-driven yield (JLP) and credit-market yield (RWAs), 'both of which can compress or disappear'. Ethena's sUSDe reward is funding and basis income that 'will vary considerably (even day to day)' and can be zero. Chaos Labs shows part of the appeal of sUSDe loops is Ethena points. A loop sized on a funding or incentive yield carries a Y that can fall to zero while B stays positive. (medium confidence)

Incentive-driven carry can disappear without a price move. Curvance's example shows a loop moving from positive to negative carry when a temporary token-reward campaign ends, so Y should be split into organic yield and rewards. (low confidence)

Published negative-carry tests compare the Aave borrow APY with the sUSDe reward yield only, so they leave out incentives that may keep loops open. Sentora's watch metric is 'Aave borrow APY minus sUSDe yield staying < 0'. CryptoSlate calls the loop negative 'before incentives, transaction costs, and other frictions'. Chaos Labs says loopers amplify 'sUSDe rewards and Ethena points', and that the liquid-leverage campaign (50% USDe, 50% sUSDe) gives 'a blended return that ultimately matches the sUSDe reward yield across their entire position', which applies Y to collateral that does not earn it unaided. None of the three quantifies the points, so whether a negative-carry loop stays open depends on a term these sources do not measure. (medium confidence)

Fixed-rate borrowing turns B into a known input for the term, at a price. Kamino says fixed-rate borrowing 'allows locking the borrow cost for the full term of a position, converting a variable-spread strategy into a predictable one', at the cost of 'typically paying a small premium over the variable rate at time of entry'. Notional charges an upfront fee on entry and on exit before maturity, and warns that its fixed borrow maturities 'may not align exactly with PT expirations': when fixed debt matures it 'converts to a variable rate', which reintroduces rate risk until the PT expires. (medium confidence)

The execution route changes both the realised entry leverage and the cost. Kamino's developer docs say manual looping takes '8-10 separate transactions', is 'Exposed to price changes between each step' and takes 'Slippage on each swap individually'. They add that if borrow rates spike mid-loop 'you may end up with a worse position than intended — or fail to complete the loop entirely'. Atomic Multiply uses one flash-loan transaction with a 'single consolidated slippage check' and a 0.001% flash-loan fee, charged on open, adjust and close. The SENTRA Fluid example models six swaps in and six out. A quoted Net APY assumes the target L and the quoted B hold at entry; the same Kamino table lists no price exposure between steps for the atomic route and exposure at each step for the manual route. (medium confidence)

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (Y−B)×(L−1): unlevered yield plus the yield spread earned on each borrowed dollar. Kamino writes it as 'Net APY = Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'. SODAX writes it as effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, where its 'leverage' is the borrowed amount per unit of deposit (that is, L−1), so the two forms are algebraically identical. Check which convention a calculator uses before comparing numbers. (high confidence)

Yield-side inputs in calculators may be trailing averages. SODAX takes the LSD staking yield from DefiLlama's latest apy value (a trailing 7-30 day window, per the SODAX doc) and falls back to a hardcoded value flagged stale:true if the fetch fails, so a calculator's Y can lag the live rate. (low confidence)

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (L−1)×(Y−B): the unlevered yield plus the spread earned on each borrowed unit. Kamino writes 'Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'; CryptoTicker writes 'result = yield + borrowed units × (yield − borrow rate)'. SODAX writes effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, but its 'leverage' is debt ÷ equity = targetLTV/(1−targetLTV) = L−1; its code comment says this is 'Not total exposure' and that a UI 'Leverage' label shows 1 + that value. Check whether a calculator's 'leverage' means L or L−1 before comparing numbers. (high confidence)

Calculator outputs differ in ways that change the answer. Kamino's open-position screen shows a Net APY indicator plus a simulation 'based on 180-day historical data' (backward-looking; the docs do not say whether Net APY itself uses spot or trailing rates). SODAX's SDK exposes two numbers: getApr() uses lending-pool rates only and can read negative, while getEffectiveApr() adds the LSD staking yield. Jupiter Lend's Liquidation Calculator estimates how long a position takes to reach liquidation under chosen borrow-rate scenarios. (medium confidence)

Kamino's Multiply interface has a Liquidation Analysis Suite that lets a user 'adjust leverage and theoretical yield to see break-even thresholds', simulate time-to-liquidation under different borrow-rate scenarios, and run historical backtests. The docs advise using it before opening any leveraged position, particularly for JLP and xStocks. They do not say whether its break-even uses the spot or a trailing B. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
